c.tagline: Nigeria's vast Yoruba metropolis of rust-red rooftops, cocoa-trade history, and its first university.

taxi.fareNote: Street and shared taxis have no meters — agree the fare before getting in. App rides (Bolt, inDrive) show an upfront price and are the easiest way to skip the haggling.

emergency.note: 112 is the national emergency line and 199 reaches police/fire; response can be slow and ambulances are scarce, so serious cases are often handled by private hospitals. Keep your hotel's and a local contact's numbers handy.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: An upscale residential and commercial district built around the sprawling Bodija Market, with banks, supermarkets, and eateries; a popular, relatively convenient base for visitors wanting shops and food with easy access across the city.

Ibadan's historic commercial core, home to the landmark Cocoa House (once tropical Africa's tallest building), the vast Dugbe Market, and Lebanon Street; central and lively but congested, best for those who want to be near business and markets.

A leafy Government Reserved Area beside Agodi Gardens and the state secretariat, with quieter tree-lined streets, government offices, and older colonial-era houses; suits travelers wanting green space and calm near the centre.
A major dual-carriageway district lined with hotels, event centres, and eateries around the Obafemi Awolowo (Liberty) Stadium; one of the better areas for dining and going out after dark.

The area around the University of Ibadan, Sango, and Ajibode, full of students, bookshops, cheap restaurants, and budget lodging; youthful, affordable, and close to the campus's zoo and botanical grounds.
lodging: Trois Ore Residences & Green Earth Bistro

water.note: Piped supply is unreliable and often contaminated; stick to bottled water.

transit.hours: Danfo minibuses, korope minivans, and keke (tricycles) run roughly 6:00 AM to around 9-10:00 PM; after dark options thin out, so app rides or a private taxi are the safer bet.
transit.note: Ibadan has no metro, tram, or city bus authority; getting around means shared 'danfo' minibuses and 'korope' minivans on fixed routes, 'keke' tricycles for short hops, okada (motorbike taxis, restricted on some roads), and app-based cars (Bolt, inDrive).
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or conductor, typically ₦100–₦500 depending on distance; there is no transit card. Keep small naira notes handy.

air: Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos (LOS) — ~2.5 hr drive, used for most international flights
bus: Intra-city danfo minibuses and korope minivans
Interstate buses to Lagos, Abuja and beyond (parks at Iwo Road, Challenge, Ojoo)
train: Lagos–Ibadan Standard Gauge Railway (Moniya station) to Lagos

transit.m: Bolt or inDrive to city center (~25-40 min)
Shared taxi/keke from Alakia junction into town
Many fly into Lagos (MMA/LOS) instead and take an intercity bus ~2.5 hr, since IBA has very few flights

tip.r: Not expected; a small 'dash' or rounding up (₦200–₦500) for good service, porters, or drivers is appreciated but never obligatory.

landmarks: Cocoa House

Once the tallest building in tropical Africa, this striking 1960s tower symbolizes Ibadan's cocoa-trading wealth and remains an iconic part of the skyline. Its rooftop offers sweeping views of the sprawling city.
Mapo Hall

Perched atop a hill in the old city, this grand colonial-era town hall with its neoclassical columns is one of Ibadan's most photographed buildings. From its steps, visitors get a stunning panorama of Ibadan's famous rust-red rooftops.
University of Ibadan
Nigeria's oldest university boasts leafy, historic grounds, striking modernist architecture, and a renowned botanical garden. It's a fascinating blend of academic heritage and green open space.
Bower's Tower (Oke-Are)

This colonial-era stone lookout tower sits atop one of Ibadan's seven hills, offering one of the best panoramic views of the city's endless terracotta rooftops. It's a favorite spot for photographers at sunset.
Agodi Gardens
A lush recreational park with landscaped gardens, a small zoo, and picnic spots, offering a relaxing green retreat from the bustling city. It's popular with families and weekend visitors.
University of Ibadan Zoological Garden
One of Nigeria's oldest zoos, home to lions, chimpanzees, and other native wildlife within the university campus. It's an easy, engaging stop for animal lovers and families.
Dugbe Market

A sprawling, chaotic, and colorful market that has anchored Ibadan's commerce for generations, selling everything from textiles to fresh produce. It's a vivid immersion into the city's everyday energy.
Oyo State Museum of Natural History
Located on the University of Ibadan campus, this museum houses an eclectic collection of natural history and cultural artifacts. It's a worthwhile stop for curious travelers wanting local context.
Oja'ba (Old Ibadan Market Quarter)

The historic core of Ibadan near the old palace, with narrow lanes, traditional compounds, and a strong sense of the city's Yoruba heritage. Wandering here reveals the layered history behind the modern metropolis.
Ibadan's Seven Hills Viewpoints

Ibadan is famously built across seven hills, and various vantage points across the city reveal an endless sea of rust-colored rooftops stretching to the horizon. It's one of the most striking urban vistas in West Africa.

dom.op: Nigerian Railway Corporation - Lagos-Ibadan Train Service

train.note: The standard-gauge Lagos-Ibadan line opened in June 2021 and is the best railway in the country, running the 157 km via Abeokuta in about 2.5 hours with a couple of round trips a day. Its Ibadan terminus is at Moniya, roughly 18 km north of the centre, so budget for a taxi at each end. Ticketing has been patchy - seats have at times been sold only for cash at the station rather than online - so arrive early or book through the LITS portal. Ibadan also sits on the old narrow-gauge Lagos-Kano line, but those services are unreliable, and no train crosses an international border.

bus.note: Shared cars and minibuses from several Lagos terminals reach Ibadan in about three hours in good traffic and arrive at the Iwo Road, Ojoo and Challenge motor parks. Branded operators including GIGM (https://gigm.com/) and ABC Transport (https://www.abctransport.com/) run to Abuja and the southeast and can be booked online; everything else is pay-at-the-park. Regional services also link Abeokuta, Ife, Oyo and Ilorin, with night departures northwards. International coaches to Ghana, Benin and Togo leave from Lagos Jibowu, not Ibadan.

ferry.note: Ibadan is an inland city about 120 km from the coast with no navigable waterway, so there are no ferry or passenger boat services; the nearest boats are the lagoon services in Lagos.

half.name: Ado Awaye Suspended Lake
half.blurb: A crater lake perched atop a hill above Ado Awaye village, reached by a steep hike, about ninety minutes from Ibadan.

full.name: Olumo Rock (Abeokuta)
full.blurb: A granite outcrop with historic Egba refuge caves and a viewing platform reached by elevator, about two hours from Ibadan.

full.name: Erin Ijesha (Olumirin) Waterfalls
full.blurb: A multi-tiered waterfall in Osun State reached by a climb up seven stepped levels, roughly two and a half hours from Ibadan.
